texts.label: text
texts.orig: Like any good researcher, I'd answer this by saying “it depends.” And it depends on many factors, but in general, I'd offer the following guidance:
texts.text: Like any good researcher, I'd answer this by saying “it depends.” And it depends on many factors, but in general, I'd offer the following guidance:

texts.label: text
texts.orig: If you can easily reach 100+ active users, consider a survey
texts.text: If you can easily reach 100+ active users, consider a survey

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Product-market fit happens only when a set of underlying assumptions end up being true. So try to break down what those assumptions might be for your product, and use questions that measure your progress toward confirming them. Ask questions along the lines of:
texts.text: Product-market fit happens only when a set of underlying assumptions end up being true. So try to break down what those assumptions might be for your product, and use questions that measure your progress toward confirming them. Ask questions along the lines of:

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: How would you feel if you could no longer use this product: Very Disappointed, Somewhat Disappointed, Not Disappointed?
texts.text: How would you feel if you could no longer use this product: Very Disappointed, Somewhat Disappointed, Not Disappointed?

texts.label: text
texts.orig: You may have already done some Googling and stumbled upon this question credited to
texts.text: You may have already done some Googling and stumbled upon this question credited to

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Sean Ellis
texts.text: Sean Ellis

texts.label: text
texts.orig: , and recently popularized by

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Rahul Vohra
texts.text: Rahul Vohra

texts.label: text
texts.orig: . Ellis claims 40% of users answering “very disappointed” is the critical threshold for his question. This directionally makes sense to me.
texts.text: . Ellis claims 40% of users answering “very disappointed” is the critical threshold for his question. This directionally makes sense to me.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Compared to other ways you do X [where X is some essential function of your product], using this product to do X is generally: Much Better, Somewhat Better, Neither better nor worse, Somewhat Worse, Much Worse?
texts.text: Compared to other ways you do X [where X is some essential function of your product], using this product to do X is generally: Much Better, Somewhat Better, Neither better nor worse, Somewhat Worse, Much Worse?

texts.label: text
texts.orig: What you’ll want to see are non-trivial skews in a positive direction towards your product — even if they’re not majorities.
texts.text: What you’ll want to see are non-trivial skews in a positive direction towards your product — even if they’re not majorities.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The last time you did X, what product or tool did you use to do it, and why? [Leave this one open ended]
texts.text: The last time you did X, what product or tool did you use to do it, and why? [Leave this one open ended]

texts.label: text
texts.orig: This third question is useful because it's behavioral. It will give you a rough signal of whether or not your product is actually being used at the times you think it should be— something your logs can't see. You’ll want to look for evidence that could suggest people are choosing an alternative to do the job you want your product to do for them. For example, if this question had revealed a plurality of early Airbnb guests saying that they had booked their last vacation on VRBO because they thought it offered more choices for non-urban travel destinations, I’d have told the co-founders that they had a problem on their hands.
texts.text: This third question is useful because it's behavioral. It will give you a rough signal of whether or not your product is actually being used at the times you think it should be— something your logs can't see. You’ll want to look for evidence that could suggest people are choosing an alternative to do the job you want your product to do for them. For example, if this question had revealed a plurality of early Airbnb guests saying that they had booked their last vacation on VRBO because they thought it offered more choices for non-urban travel destinations, I’d have told the co-founders that they had a problem on their hands.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Ellis' question is a measure of user affection for your product, the second question is a measure of relative utility, and like I said the third is behavioral.
texts.text: Ellis' question is a measure of user affection for your product, the second question is a measure of relative utility, and like I said the third is behavioral.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: While product-market fit looks different for every product, it’s hard to imagine a scenario where you’ll attain PMF if people don’t feel some degree of affection for your product, don’t find it useful, and don’t use it 😉
texts.text: While product-market fit looks different for every product, it’s hard to imagine a scenario where you’ll attain PMF if people don’t feel some degree of affection for your product, don’t find it useful, and don’t use it 😉

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Despite all the easy ways to build and launch a survey these days, they might not always be feasible, so:
texts.text: Despite all the easy ways to build and launch a survey these days, they might not always be feasible, so:

texts.label: text
texts.orig: If you can't easily survey 100+ active users, talk to 6-12 of them
texts.text: If you can't easily survey 100+ active users, talk to 6-12 of them

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Ask questions along the lines of:
texts.text: Ask questions along the lines of:

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: Walk me through the last time you did X [where X is some essential function of your product]. For each key decision you made along the way, tell me a bit about why you made those decisions.
texts.text: Walk me through the last time you did X [where X is some essential function of your product]. For each key decision you made along the way, tell me a bit about why you made those decisions.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: You’ll notice this question doesn’t even refer to your product at all – ask it to understand how people typically go about the key task your product is meant to enable. Then ask the following questions to see how well-suited your product is to replacing or improving that work.
texts.text: You’ll notice this question doesn’t even refer to your product at all – ask it to understand how people typically go about the key task your product is meant to enable. Then ask the following questions to see how well-suited your product is to replacing or improving that work.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: What are the different products you use to do X? What are the best and worst parts of using those products? The last time you did X using this product, why did you use it instead of something else?
texts.text: What are the different products you use to do X? What are the best and worst parts of using those products? The last time you did X using this product, why did you use it instead of something else?

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Again, where X is some essential function of your product.
texts.text: Again, where X is some essential function of your product.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Why did you try this product in the first place? What were you hoping it would do for you? How well has it delivered on that hope?
texts.text: Why did you try this product in the first place? What were you hoping it would do for you? How well has it delivered on that hope?

texts.label: text
texts.orig: You’ll want to keep an ear out for two things that may signal product-market fit:
texts.text: You’ll want to keep an ear out for two things that may signal product-market fit:

texts.label: text
texts.orig: a recognition of explicit, superior value relative to competitors or alternatives, and genuine enthusiasm.
texts.text: a recognition of explicit, superior value relative to competitors or alternatives, and genuine enthusiasm.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: There should be clear, qualitative daylight between the ways that people talk about using your product and the ways they use alternatives, and people should have no trouble articulating detailed specifics of why your product is preferable.
texts.text: There should be clear, qualitative daylight between the ways that people talk about using your product and the ways they use alternatives, and people should have no trouble articulating detailed specifics of why your product is preferable.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: There should also be an element of excitement.
texts.text: There should also be an element of excitement.

texts.orig: NPS (Net Promoter Score), or "How likely are you to recommend this product to a friend?

texts.label: text
texts.orig: While touted as a panacea by what a former Airbnb colleague calls "the NPS Industrial Complex," both the underlying science and the practical utility of this question are debatable at best.
texts.text: While touted as a panacea by what a former Airbnb colleague calls "the NPS Industrial Complex," both the underlying science and the practical utility of this question are debatable at best.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: What people want, so that you can go blindly build it
texts.text: What people want, so that you can go blindly build it

texts.label: text
texts.orig: This is why you'll rarely hear user researchers wasting energy debating the tired old tropes about how Henry Ford or Steve Jobs would never listen to research: it's just blatantly, obviously true that people sometimes don't know what they want until they see it. Asking people what they want isn't research.

Asking people what they want isn't research.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: So, as I said at the outset, there are many questions you can ask...but there's no magic single question that’ll tell you everything you want to know. Using multiple approaches and triangulating between them is your best bet.
texts.text: So, as I said at the outset, there are many questions you can ask...but there's no magic single question that’ll tell you everything you want to know. Using multiple approaches and triangulating between them is your best bet.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: As you collect data, you should be trying to falsify your product's underlying assumptions
texts.text: As you collect data, you should be trying to falsify your product's underlying assumptions

texts.label: text
texts.orig: : is it true that people are experiencing the problem your product sets out to solve in the first place? What motivated them to try it in the first place? What was the magical way in which they were hoping it might make their life or some task even a little bit better? Understanding people's motivations for using what you've built can sometimes be surprising, but can also lead you down unexpected new paths to achieving a strong product-market fit.
